turns.speaker: A
turns.text: We all dream, but why? Does science have an answer?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Honestly, there's no single answer yet. But scientists have learned a lot. For example, our most vivid, story-like dreams usually happen during REM sleep. REM stands for rapid eye movement, because our eyes move quickly under our eyelids.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: In cycles through the night, about every ninety minutes. The REM periods get longer toward the morning. That's why we often remember dreams just before we wake up.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So what are the main theories?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: One popular idea is about memory. During sleep, the brain seems to sort and store what we learned during the day. Dreams might be a side effect of that process, mixing new and old memories.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That explains why dreams can be so strange.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. Another theory is emotional processing. Dreams may help us deal with strong feelings, like fear or sadness, in a safe environment.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Some researchers think dreams let us practice responding to threats. Others argue that dreams are simply the brain's attempt to make a story out of random activity during sleep.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Possibly several of them. Dreaming may have more than one purpose. It's one of the most fascinating open questions in neuroscience.
